\chapter{The Two Hearts}
\label{ch:ml-two-hearts}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name my heart in Malayalam two ways, one Sanskrit and one native, and say which one everyday idiom actually uses and why hridayam is a genuine cousin of the English word heart.}

Name hridayam and nenchu, place nenchidippu beside the santosham/nandi pattern from Chapter 2, and trace hridayam's root to the same PIE ancestor as English heart.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hṛdayaṁ]{\ml{ഹൃദയം} (hṛdayaṁ) — \textquotedblleft{}heart,\textquotedblright{} a cousin of the English word}

\label{lesson:ML-C38-hrudayam}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Suhṛttŭ}, \textquotedblleft{}friend,\textquotedblright{} was built on \textbf{hṛd}, \textquotedblleft{}heart\textquotedblright{} — a piece promised, not yet taught. Here it is, whole.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഹൃദയം}} — \emph{hṛdayaṁ} — \textbf{heart}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{എന്റെ} \ml{ഹൃദയം}.} — \emph{ente hṛdayaṁ.} — \textquotedblleft{}My heart.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{ഹൃദയം}} is Sanskrit \textbf{\dv{हृदय}} (\emph{hṛdaya}), \textquotedblleft{}heart,\textquotedblright{} absorbed with the same nativizing \textbf{‑\ml{അം}} you already met on \textbf{\ml{കുടുംബം}} and \textbf{\ml{ഇഷ്ടം}}. Its root, \textbf{\dv{हृद्}} (\emph{hṛd}), is not just Indo-\emph{Aryan} but Indo-\emph{European}: the same ancient root that gave Greek \textbf{kardía}, Latin \textbf{cor/cordis}, and — by a long chain of regular sound changes inside Germanic — English \textbf{heart} itself. \emph{Hṛdayaṁ} and \textquotedblleft{}heart\textquotedblright{} are genuine cousins, distant but real, through Sanskrit's own branch of the family tree English belongs to. That resemblance is a coincidence of deep history, not of Malayalam's own Dravidian family — Dravidian and Indo-European share no common ancestor at all.

\emph{Suhṛttŭ}, \textquotedblleft{}friend,\textquotedblright{} is this very root wearing \textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{} in front of it — \textbf{su} + \textbf{hṛd}, good-heart.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ente hṛdayaṁ\textquotedblright{} — my heart
  \item the distant cousins — \textquotedblleft{}hṛdaya … kardía … cor … heart\textquotedblright{}
  \item the friend-word, taken apart again — \textquotedblleft{}su + hṛd\textquotedblright{}
  \item mouth, then heart — \textquotedblleft{}vāy … hṛdayaṁ\textquotedblright{}
  \item all the face words once more — \textquotedblleft{}kaṇṇŭ, cevi, mūkkŭ, vāy\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}my heart.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Ente hṛdayaṁ}.) Is \emph{hṛdayaṁ} a Dravidian word or a Sanskrit one? (\textbf{Sanskrit}, dressed in Malayalam's own \emph{‑aṁ}.) Name an English word that is a genuine, if distant, cousin of \emph{hṛd}. (\textbf{Heart} — both from the same PIE root, by way of Greek \emph{kardía} and Latin \emph{cor}.) Which earlier word was built on this same root? (\emph{\textbf{\ml{സുഹൃത്ത്}}} — \emph{su} \textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{} + \emph{hṛd} \textquotedblleft{}heart.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nenchŭ]{\ml{നെഞ്ച്} (nenchŭ) — \textquotedblleft{}chest,\textquotedblright{} Malayalam's other heart}

\label{lesson:ML-C38-nenchu}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഹൃദയം}} was borrowed, formal, and shared with English by deep ancestry. This chapter's second word is none of those three things.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{നെഞ്ച്}} — \emph{nenchŭ} — \textbf{chest}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{എന്റെ} \ml{നെഞ്ച്}.} — \emph{ente nenchŭ.} — \textquotedblleft{}My chest.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{നെഞ്ച്}} is native Dravidian, cognate with Tamil's own \textbf{\ta{நெஞ்சு}/\ta{நெஞ்சம்}} (\emph{nenju/nenjam}), \textquotedblleft{}chest.\textquotedblright{} Where \textbf{\ml{ഹൃദയം}} names the organ and carries the Sanskrit-flavoured abstraction — a \textquotedblleft{}heartfelt\textquotedblright{} thank-you, a broken heart in the literary sense — \textbf{\ml{നെഞ്ച്}} is the word everyday idiom actually reaches for: \textbf{\ml{നെഞ്ചിടിപ്പ്}} (\emph{nenchiṭippŭ}), a heart pounding from fear or excitement, literally \textquotedblleft{}chest-beat.\textquotedblright{}

Two hearts, then: one Sanskrit and formal, one native and physical. That is the same selective-borrowing pattern Chapter 2 already showed with \textbf{\ml{സന്തോഷം}} beside \textbf{\ml{നന്ദി}} — Malayalam does not simply prefer Sanskrit or prefer native; it keeps both, and lets register decide which one a given sentence reaches for. \textbf{\ml{തല}} and \textbf{\ml{കൈ}}, this stretch's first two body words, were native throughout; \textbf{\ml{ഹൃദയം}} and \textbf{\ml{നെഞ്ച്}} show the same body carrying one word of each kind, side by side.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ente nenchŭ\textquotedblright{} — my chest
  \item two hearts — \textquotedblleft{}hṛdayaṁ,\textquotedblright{} formal; \textquotedblleft{}nenchŭ,\textquotedblright{} everyday
  \item the idiom — \textquotedblleft{}nenchiṭippŭ\textquotedblright{} — chest-beat, a pounding heart
  \item thala, kai, hṛdayaṁ, nenchŭ — the body words so far
  \item mouth, once more — \textquotedblleft{}vāy\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}my chest.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Ente nenchŭ}.) Which of this chapter's two heart-words is native, and which is borrowed? (\textbf{\ml{നെഞ്ച്}} native; \textbf{\ml{ഹൃദയം}} Sanskrit.) What does \emph{nenchiṭippŭ} mean, literally? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Chest-beat\textquotedblright{}} — a pounding heart.) Which earlier pair showed this same native-plus-Sanskrit side-by-side pattern? (\textbf{\ml{സന്തോഷം} beside \ml{നന്ദി}}, Chapter 2.)
\end{tcolorbox}
